stops.name: Puerto de la Hambre, the first voyage's hunger
stops.campa: The first voyage south, a hundred and twelve men and a scatter of horses, crawls down an uncharted coast of mangrove and rain past Puerto Piñas and the Colombian rivers, and comes at last to a bay of driven famine the company names, without irony, Puerto de la Hambre: the Port of Hunger. Provisions fail; the relief ship does not come; men eat shellfish, roots, the flesh of their own dead. More than twenty starve outright. Pizarro holds the survivors together on this shore by will alone, waiting on a ship that is late by months, not days.

stops.name: Isla del Gallo, the line in the sand, the Thirteen of Fame
stops.campa: Marooned on this mangrove islet while Almagro begs reinforcements in Panamá, the company mutinies against another season of hunger and fever. The relief ship of Governor Ríos comes not with men but an order home. Pizarro draws a single line in the wet sand with the point of his sword, and turns to face them: on that side, Panamá, and poverty; on this side, the south, and what it holds. He steps across his own line first. Thirteen men, the Thirteen of Fame, cross after him. The rest sail home to safety and the tradition's contempt.
stops.quote: There lies Peru with its riches; here, Panamá and its poverty. Choose, each man, what best becomes a brave Castilian. For my part, I go to the south.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by tradition (Gómara, Historia General de las Indias; Zárate; popularized in Prescott, History of the Conquest of Peru, 1847)

stops.name: Tumbes, the first sight of the empire
stops.campa: The pilot Bartolomé Ruiz, sailing on ahead, has already taken a balsa raft of Tumbes traders off the coast: cotton cloth, worked silver, gold ornaments, emeralds, proof at last that the rumor was true. Now Pizarro's own remaining company sails into the bay of Tumbes and finds a stone-built town of terraced fields, canals, a fortress and a temple of the Sun, subjects of a lord called the Inca whose empire, the Tumbes people say, runs the length of the mountains to the south. Thirteen starving men have found, at last, the kingdom the whole voyage was staked on.

stops.name: Toledo, the Capitulación, before the absent Emperor
stops.campa: Pizarro crosses the Ocean again, this time to the Emperor's own court, to lay Tumbes and the balsa's gold before Charles V. The Emperor is elsewhere; the Empress Isabella signs in Toledo the Capitulación that makes Pizarro governor, captain general, adelantado for life of New Castile, the two hundred leagues of coast from the Santiago River to Chincha, with a knighthood of Santiago besides. Almagro, his partner of five years' hunger, receives the lesser governorship of Tumbes alone; Luque is named bishop. The document that will conquer an empire also plants, in its unequal shares, the seed of a civil war.

stops.name: Trujillo, recruiting the brothers of his blood
stops.campa: Before sailing back he returns once more to Trujillo, the town that never troubled to know him as a boy, and gathers to the enterprise the men of his own blood: his half-brothers Hernando, Juan, and Gonzalo Pizarro, and his half-brother by another line, Francisco Martín de Alcántara. Extremadura sends four brothers across the Ocean on the strength of one bastard's royal grant, the same soil that will one day send Hernán Cortés's own kin, and the tradition binds the two conquerors as cousins of a single hard country. All four will die in Peru; none of natural causes.

stops.name: Nombre de Dios, landfall from Spain, the quarrel with Almagro
stops.campa: Returning from Spain with his royal patents and his brothers, Pizarro makes landfall at Nombre de Dios, the Caribbean door of the isthmus, where Almagro comes hurrying to meet him, and finds the pact of equal thirds signed away at Toledo: governor, captain general, adelantado, all of it Pizarro's, and for himself only Tumbes. The quarrel flares hot on the very beach; Almagro must be talked back into the enterprise with promises of titles still unwon. The partnership survives its first wound. It will not survive the empire the wound is carried into.

stops.name: Panamá, the banners blessed, the third fleet sails
stops.campa: In the church of La Merced at Panamá, the same Mercedarian church where the pact of three was sworn six years before, the expedition hears mass and has its banners blessed on the feast-heavy end of December, 1530. In the first days of January the three ships stand out from the Pacific port at last: about a hundred and eighty men, a few dozen horses, the Pizarro brothers all aboard, Almagro left behind once more to raise reinforcements and follow. It is the third sailing south, and the one the Capitulación has armed with an empire's paper title.

stops.name: San Miguel de Tangarará, the first Spanish town in Peru
stops.campa: On the banks of the Chira, Pizarro founds San Miguel: the third Spanish city of South America and the first in Peru, a cabildo, a church, a garrison of the halt and the sick left behind when the main column marches inland. He has landed already into a kingdom split by civil war: the emperor Huáscar defeated and held by his half-brother Atahualpa, whose armies have not yet turned to notice the hundred and sixty foreigners now walking, on foot and on unfamiliar horses, straight toward the high sierra where Atahualpa camps with his court.

stops.name: Cajamarca, the envoys at Atahualpa's baths
stops.campa: The column of a hundred and sixty enters the empty city of Cajamarca and finds the Inca's army, tens of thousands strong, encamped in tents on the hillside above, at the hot springs where Atahualpa is taking his ease after the defeat of Huáscar. Hernando de Soto and then Hernando Pizarro ride out to the camp, deliver Francisco's invitation to a meeting in the plaza, and return awed by what they have seen: an army beyond counting, and an Inca who receives armed strangers on horseback without rising from his golden stool.

stops.name: Cajamarca, the ambush in the plaza, Atahualpa seized
stops.campa: Atahualpa enters the great plaza at dusk on a litter of gold, borne by his lords, with several thousand unarmed attendants singing before him. Friar Vicente de Valverde comes out with cross and missal and calls on him to accept the faith and the Emperor; Atahualpa turns the book in his hands, finds it dumb, and throws it to the ground. At the signal a cannon fires and the cry of Santiago goes up from every doorway; cavalry and gunfire break into the unarmed crowd, and in less than an hour thousands lie dead in the plaza. Pizarro himself, sword drawn, seizes Atahualpa from his fallen litter and takes him prisoner with his own hand.
stops.quote: And if you were taken prisoner, and your people defeated and killed, it was because you came with so great an army against us, when we came to ask that you come in peace — and you threw to the ground the book in which are the words of God; for this our Lord permitted that your pride be brought low.
stops.quote_source: Francisco de Xérez, secretary to Pizarro, Verdadera relación de la conquista del Perú (1534)

stops.name: Cajamarca, the ransom promised, a room to be filled
stops.campa: From his captivity Atahualpa offers his own price for freedom: he will fill the long chamber where he is held with gold as high as a man can reach on the wall, and two smaller adjoining rooms with silver, twice over. Runners go out from Cajamarca to every shrine and palace of the empire; llama trains begin arriving from Cusco with plate stripped from the Coricancha itself. Pizarro accepts the bargain and waits, months on end, while the greatest ransom in the history of the world accumulates, plank by golden plank, inside the room the Inca measured with his own raised hand.

stops.name: Cajamarca, the room filled once with gold
stops.campa: By late spring the chamber stands filled to the mark Atahualpa set with his own hand: plate, vessels, idols, and ornament of gold from every temple of the empire, weighed and melted down by the royal smiths under guard. It is, the chroniclers agree, the richest single ransom ever paid on earth: some six thousand pounds of gold delivered for the freedom of one man. Pizarro sets aside the royal fifth for the Crown and divides the rest among the company by rank, from the horsemen down to the sick left behind at San Miguel, who each still draw a share.
